doc.title: Junior Mance Part I interviewed by Monk Rowe and Michael Woods, New York City, New York, July 27, 1995 [interview 1 of 2]

title: Teaching a blues class
summary: How Mance approaches teaching blues: forms, chord sheets, records and singers in the class.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Becoming a teacher: jazz in schools and conservatories

blocks.x: Let me ask you a question about this blues class. Tell me some of the things you teach people to sensitize them to play the blues with a feeling.

Well, that’s a big problem, sensitizing them to play the blues. Well to begin with, they have to be sophomores to take this class. In order to get into the blues they have to have a musical background anyway, I mean everybody is auditioned. You can be a hell of a classical musician or something but if you don’t know the basics about playing jazz, you know they tell you well go and get that together and then come back. So as I said, when they asked me to do it, I said how do you teach anybody to play the blues? They said oh, I’m sure you’ll find a way. But what I do is I usually start off to see if they know all the forms like the 12-bar blues form or the 8-bar blues form, 16-bar blues forms, you know and I go by like from what I’ve heard different blues singers, the structures that they sing off mostly, you know, all the old timers. And I make up chord sheets, you know and I pass them out to everybody so that they all have them to get familiar with. Because many, many 12-bar blues forms, there’s a lot of them, there’s the minor blues and then there’s three or four different kind of minor blues forms. And three or four different ways of doing major blues. And I start with that which usually doesn’t take long, because usually they are advanced enough to know that and they have no trouble reading the chord sheets. And the rest is all performing. And there is usually two or three singers in the class. And I

use a lot of records, I bring records to class, we have equipment there to play records or CDs on, and usually I’ve been lucky so far, most of them when they get there they know what they want, where they’re going, they know what they want. They’re not just strictly a neophyte as far as the word “blues” is concerned. And so and I love it. They told me, they says, well try it for a few weeks and if you don’t like it we will understand. I’ve been there six years and going into my seventh year, and it’s really great.
